ai.glance: Munch created four versions of this iconic image after experiencing an 'infinite scream passing through nature' during a sunset walk. The agonized face became an icon of existential dread and inspired its own emoji.

story.receipt: Munch's journal, January 22, 1892: 'I was walking along the road with two friends-the sun was setting-suddenly the sky turned blood red-I paused, feeling exhausted, and leaned on the fence-there was blood and tongues of fire above the blue-black fjord and the city-my friends walked on, and I stood there trembling with anxiety-and I sensed an infinite scream passing through nature.'
story.surface_layer: A figure stands on a boardwalk at the edge of a fjord, hands pressed to its skull-like face, mouth and eyes wide in horror. The figure's body undulates like the landscape behind it-both seem to vibrate with the same unseen force. Orange and red clouds streak across the sky like blood, reflecting in the blue-black water below. Two figures walk away in the background, oblivious. A railing leads the eye into the depth, toward a distant cityscape.
story.type_aesthetic: Symbolist-Expressionist painting using tempera and pastel on cardboard (in the 1893 version). Wavy, sinuous lines derived from Art Nouveau create visual anxiety. The landscape echoes the figure's emotional state-external nature made internal. Palette of complementary oranges and blues creates maximum chromatic tension.
story.core_philosophy: Anxiety as universal experience. The figure does not scream but receives a scream-nature itself screams through this hollow vessel. Munch transforms personal terror into an image of modern alienation that resonates across cultures and centuries.
story.cultural_context: Created in 1893 during the Symbolist movement, when artists across Europe rejected naturalism to explore psychology, spirituality, and inner experience. Munch was haunted by death-his mother died when he was five, his sister Sophie at fifteen. He later wrote: 'Illness, insanity, and death were the black angels that kept watch over my cradle.' The painting emerged from a period of intense psychological crisis in Berlin and Kristiania (Oslo).

observation_details.label: The Figure
observation_details.value: Genderless, almost fetal-Munch removes individual identity to create universal symbol. The face echoes a Peruvian mummy Munch saw at the Paris Exposition

observation_details.label: The Sky
observation_details.value: The blood-red clouds may depict volcanic sunsets following Krakatoa's 1883 eruption, visible in Norway through 1884

observation_details.label: The Location
observation_details.value: Ekeberg hill overlooking Kristiania (Oslo), near both a slaughterhouse (screams of animals) and an asylum where Munch's sister was confined

observation_details.label: Four Versions
observation_details.value: Munch created four versions: two pastels (1893, 1895), one tempera (1893, at National Museum), one tempera (1910, at Munch Museum)
